lines: This is Switzerland, seen from space.
A small country in the middle of Europe, with no coast, almost no oil or coal, and mountains almost everywhere.
Yet it is one of the richest countries on Earth.
In twenty twenty-four, it produced about one hundred seven thousand dollars of goods and services for every person living there.
That is about eight times the world average, and almost twice as much as its big neighbour, Germany.
But two hundred years ago, this was a poor country.
In the hungry year of eighteen seventeen, some people here ate grass to survive.
So how does a mountain country with almost nothing become this rich?
The short answer: it learned to sell things that weigh almost nothing.
First, where is it?
Switzerland sits in the heart of Europe, between Germany, France, Italy, Austria, and tiny Liechtenstein.
It covers about forty-one thousand square kilometres, roughly the size of the Netherlands.
About nine million people live there.
Almost sixty percent of the country is the Alps: steep slopes, long winters, and little flat land to farm.
Only about a quarter of the Swiss live up there.
It also has no sea.
Ships can reach it only by sailing up the river Rhine, hundreds of kilometres from the North Sea.
Underground, there is no oil field, no gas, and no coal mine worth mentioning.
Today, Switzerland imports almost all the oil and gas it uses.
What it does have is water.
Rain and snow feed rivers and dams, and hydropower makes about fifty-eight percent of its electricity.
Small, landlocked, mountainous, and no fuel. On paper, that is a recipe for staying poor.
For centuries, one of the things Switzerland sold abroad was its young men.
Swiss soldiers fought in foreign armies, for foreign kings, for money.
After a heavy defeat at Marignano, in fifteen fifteen, the Swiss slowly stopped fighting wars of conquest of their own.
This stone lion in Lucerne honours Swiss guards who died defending the king of France, in Paris, in seventeen ninety-two.
Then, in eighteen fifteen, a volcano called Tambora erupted in Indonesia, on the other side of the world.
Its ash and gas cooled the climate.
In Switzerland, the summer of eighteen sixteen was about two and a half degrees colder than normal.
Between May and July, it rained on fifty days out of ninety.
Harvests failed.
Food prices exploded.
A painted price board from eastern Switzerland shows a sack of grain at about fourteen gulden in eighteen eleven.
By June eighteen seventeen, the same sack cost one hundred six gulden.
That is more than seven times as much.
In the east of the country, people ate grass.
In parts of Appenzell, deaths almost tripled in eighteen seventeen.
Many families sold everything and left for America.
It was the first big wave of Swiss emigration in that century.
So far: a poor mountain country that exported soldiers and emigrants.
But one city had already found a better export.
In the fifteen hundreds, the reformer John Calvin made Geneva a strict Protestant city that frowned on luxury, including jewellery.
So Geneva's goldsmiths turned to making watches instead, helped by Protestant refugees from France who knew the craft.
This watch was made in Geneva around sixteen fifty, by Jean Rousseau.
Its case is cut from rock crystal. Small enough for a pocket, and made to be precious.
By around seventeen eighty-five, about twenty thousand people worked in watchmaking in Geneva, making eighty-five thousand watches a year.
Watchmaking spread into the Jura mountains.
By tradition, farmers there worked on watch parts during their long, snowy winters.
Here is why that matters.
In twenty twenty-four, the average Swiss watch was exported for about eighteen hundred dollars. The average Chinese watch, for about four dollars.
China exported almost forty times more watches.
But Switzerland earned more than ten times as much money from its watches.
That is the trick.
If your country is hard to reach, sell things that are small, light, and expensive. Then transport costs barely matter.
Swiss watch exports were worth about twenty-six billion francs in twenty twenty-four.
That is roughly two thousand nine hundred francs for every person in the country.
So far: Switzerland got richer by exporting small, valuable things that are cheap to move.
But to sell anything, you need a way through the mountains.
Already in the thirteenth century, mules carried goods over the Gotthard Pass, between northern Europe and Italy.
In eighteen eighty-two, a railway tunnel opened under the pass, fifteen kilometres long.
Workers spent about ten years digging it through solid rock.
In its first full year, about three hundred thousand tonnes of goods went through.
Trade that once went around the Alps could now go straight through Switzerland.
In twenty sixteen, a new tunnel opened deep below the old one: fifty-seven kilometres long, the longest railway tunnel in the world.
Switzerland had one more advantage: peace.
In eighteen fifteen, after Napoleon's wars, Europe's great powers recognised it as permanently neutral.
Even today, Switzerland is not a member of the European Union, or of any military alliance.
Switzerland stayed out of both world wars and was not invaded, while much of Europe was left in ruins.
And peace is good for money.
If you were rich and worried about war, where would you keep your savings?
So far: tunnels connected Switzerland to Europe, and neutrality kept it out of war.
Swiss banks offered stability and a strong currency.
And in nineteen thirty-four, a new law made it a crime for bankers to reveal their clients' secrets.
That attracted honest savers, but also people hiding money from the tax offices of their own countries.
Under pressure from abroad, that changed.
Since twenty eighteen, Switzerland automatically shares foreign clients' bank data with their home tax offices.
In twenty twenty-three, Credit Suisse, one of Switzerland's two biggest banks, lost the trust of its clients.
It was taken over by its rival, UBS, with guarantees from the Swiss government.
Still, Switzerland is the world leader in managing money for private clients from abroad: about two thousand four hundred billion francs in twenty twenty-four.
But here is the surprise.
Banks and insurance together make only about nine percent of the Swiss economy.
So banks matter, but they are not the main reason.
The biggest Swiss export is something you can swallow.
So far: Swiss banks are famous, but finance is only about a tenth of the economy.
This is Basel, on the Rhine, where Switzerland meets France and Germany.
In the nineteenth century, its factories made artificial dyes to colour silk and cloth.
A surprising detail: until nineteen hundred seven, Switzerland had no patent law.
So Basel firms could legally copy dyes invented abroad.
The chemists who knew how to make colours learned to make medicines.
In eighteen ninety-six, Roche was founded in Basel, making medicines only.
At Sandoz, another Basel dye maker, medicines were only ten percent of sales in nineteen fourteen. By nineteen fifty-two, they were the biggest part.
Today, Basel is home to two global drug companies, Roche and Novartis.
And chemicals and medicines are by far Switzerland's biggest export.
In twenty twenty-four, they made up about fifty-three percent of all Swiss exports: about one hundred forty-nine billion francs.
That is roughly sixteen thousand five hundred francs for every person in Switzerland, from chemicals and medicines alone.
And medicine follows the same rule as watches: small, light, valuable packages, easy to ship from the middle of a continent.
So far: Basel turned dye chemistry into medicine, now over half of Swiss exports.
The last ingredient is people.
About two thirds of young people in Switzerland choose an apprenticeship: part school, part paid training inside a real company.
There are about two hundred fifty trades to choose from.
And youth unemployment is lower than the averages of the European Union and of rich countries.
Skilled workers can make expensive products, and expensive products can pay high wages.
Now imagine you live there, with a full-time job and the median wage: about seven thousand francs a month before tax, in twenty twenty-four.
That is more than eighty-four thousand francs a year.
Sounds great. But roughly a third of household income goes to taxes and compulsory health insurance.
And prices are high.
In twenty twenty-five, everyday household spending cost about seventy percent more than the European Union average.
Still, after paying for everything, the average household saves about seventeen hundred francs a month.
So far: Swiss wages are high, but so are taxes, insurance, and prices.
Over fifty years, the gap between Switzerland and the world average grew and grew.
The line jumps up and down partly because exchange rates move. But the direction is clear.
So, why is Switzerland so rich? There is no single secret.
Mountains made it poor, so it learned to sell small, valuable things.
Tunnels connected it to Europe. Peace kept its factories and savings safe. And skilled people keep the value high.
There is a price too: life is expensive, and the country depends heavily on a few industries, above all medicine.
Here is my question for you: which country should we explain next?
Tell us in the comments.
